bull_thesis: Comcast at $23.63 is a company that just announced its own breakup, and the market shrugged. On June 29, 2026 the board committed to a tax-free spin-off (a separation that hands shareholders stock in both companies without a tax bill) of the entire NBCUniversal media business — Universal theme parks, the film and television studios, NBC, Telemundo, Bravo, the Peacock streaming service — together with Sky in Europe, expected to complete around mid-2027, with co-CEO Mike Cavanagh leading the media company and former CFO Michael Angelakis returning to run the remaining broadband company. The stock popped from $23.17 to $24.55 on the news and then gave the entire gain back within a week; at today's price the market is paying roughly 4.9 times enterprise value to operating cash earnings for the whole conglomerate — a cable-sector multiple stamped across roughly $12 billion of estimated theme-park, studio, streaming and Sky earnings that comparable media assets are valued at nearly double that. And this is not a broken business begging for a rescue: first-quarter 2026 broadband subscriber losses improved by more than 100,000 year over year, the first improvement since late 2020; wireless posted its best quarterly additions ever after adding roughly 1.5 million lines in 2025 to pass 9 million; Peacock added 2 million subscribers with revenue up more than 70% and management guiding to its first-ever profitable quarter in the report due July 23, 2026; the parks crossed $1 billion of quarterly operating earnings for the first time in late 2025 on the strength of Epic Universe; and the company's 'legendary February' (Winter Olympics, Super Bowl 60, NBA All-Star game) sold roughly $2 billion of advertising in 17 days. Management's word has been good: the Versant cable-networks spin announced in late 2024 was delivered on schedule, the company has beaten earnings estimates in every one of the last seven-plus quarters, and the operating deterioration it warned about was pre-announced, not discovered. While waiting for the separation, shareholders collect a $1.32 annual dividend (about a 5.6% yield) covered roughly four times by free cash flow, plus continued heavy share repurchases that have shrunk the share count from about 4.6 billion in 2021 to about 3.57 billion today. The conditions that must hold: the spin completes on its stated roughly one-year timeline, broadband subscriber trends keep inflecting as the free-mobile-line cohorts convert to paid in the second half of 2026, and the media assets attract media-market multiples once freed from the cable wrapper — a live proposition given the current deal frenzy (Sky itself just agreed to buy ITV's broadcast business for up to 1.6 billion pounds, and Warner Bros. Discovery spent the spring being fought over).
bear_thesis: The cheapness has an explanation, and the explanation is getting worse before it gets better. First, the sector context is brutal: Charter — the closest pure comparable — has collapsed roughly 67% from its 52-week high to a $18.6 billion market value, and small-cap Cable One has lost about 80%, because fiber overbuilders, fixed-wireless carriers and now satellite entrants are attacking the cable broadband franchise simultaneously. Comcast's own management concedes the point: 'most of our footprint will eventually be overbuilt' (Q3 2025 call). Second, the earnings are falling right now, by design: 2026 is management's self-declared 'largest broadband investment year in our history', connectivity operating earnings fell 3.7% in Q3 2025 with management guiding the decline to build 'over the next several quarters', and adjusted earnings per share dropped about 28% year over year in Q1 2026 (to $0.79 from $1.09), with the July 23 quarter expected down roughly 22% more. Third, the screener's headline cheapness is overstated: the +30% fiscal-2025 earnings growth and the $5.39 reported earnings figure lean on one-time tax benefits and gains — the adjusted quarterly series was essentially flat in 2025 at about $4.30 — and trailing free cash flow of $20.4 billion embeds new federal cash-tax savings, so the true margin of safety is meaningfully smaller than the optical 127%. Fourth, the balance sheet cuts both ways: $85.1 billion of net debt (recomputed from the March 2026 balance sheet) against roughly $34-35 billion of operating cash earnings means every half-turn the market takes off the consolidated multiple removes roughly $4-5 per share of equity value — the solvency screen (Altman-Z 1.4) flags exactly this leverage, and how the debt gets split between the two companies is not yet disclosed. Fifth, the governance lever is one-way: the Roberts family's supervoting stock makes activism impossible, so if management's timeline slips there is no outside mechanism to force it. Sixth, insiders are not buying: zero open-market purchases against three sales in the measured window. What would confirm the bear: a July 23 print showing broadband losses re-accelerating or free-line conversions disappointing, a spin timeline slipping past mid-2027, or dividend policy for the two successor companies arriving lighter than income holders expect — the 5.6% yield base is a mechanical-selling risk if the payout is restructured in the separation.
sop_breakdown: Sum-of-the-parts (valuing each business line separately), built along the announced separation line, on roughly 3.57 billion shares. Segment operating-earnings figures are estimated from call commentary and prior-year public disclosures — the inputs provide segment revenue only (fiscal 2025: residential connectivity $70.7B, media $27.1B, studios $11.3B, business services $10.2B, theme parks $9.8B). Base case: (1) The remaining broadband company (domestic residential and business connectivity, wireless) on an estimated $21.5 billion of 2026 operating cash earnings at 5.25 times enterprise value to those earnings — calibrated against Charter's live roughly 5 times, with Comcast earning a modest premium for far lower leverage and inflecting subscriber trends — is worth about $113 billion. (2) The media spin-off (Universal parks estimated $3.8B of operating earnings at 9.5 times, studios $1.5B at 8 times, NBC/Peacock media plus Sky roughly $6.5B at 5.5-6 times, less standalone overhead) sums to about $84 billion — a blended 7.3 times that sits well below where Disney trades and below what the current media deal wave is paying. (3) Corporate drag and estimated separation costs subtract about $6 billion. Total enterprise value about $193 billion, less $85.1 billion net debt, leaves roughly $106-108 billion of equity, or about $30 per share. The adverse case ($20) assumes the cable de-rate deepens toward Charter's trough treatment (4.5 times on $21 billion) and the media assets price at 6 times into an ad downturn — slightly below the June 2026 washout low of $22.13. The favorable case ($40) assumes the separation completes cleanly, the media company re-rates toward 9 times in a bid-heavy market, and the broadband company at 6 times regains consolidation optionality (press reporting on July 10, 2026 already has Comcast eyeing Charter). For reference, the base case sits just below the analyst consensus target of about $31 and far below the screener's $54 fair-value anchor, which we discount as inflated by one-time-boosted earnings.
risk_reward: Downside in an adverse scenario is anchored around $20 — just under the $22.13 June 2026 low the stock set before the separation was announced — driven by the live risk that the whole cable sector keeps de-rating the way Charter and Cable One already have. Upside to the base-case sum-of-the-parts is about $30, with the favorable case near $40 if the media company re-rates in the current deal environment. The leverage is the swing factor in both directions: with $85 billion of net debt, small changes in the multiple the market pays for the operating earnings move the equity disproportionately. A 5.6% dividend yield, covered roughly four times by free cash flow, pays the holder to wait out the roughly one-year separation timeline; the near-term risk is concentrated in the July 23, 2026 earnings print, which lands in the declared trough of the investment cycle.
peer_comps_note: The house peer set is Charter, Cable One, Disney, Warner Bros. Discovery, Verizon and AT&T, with a prior verdict that Comcast trades in line with Charter once leverage and growth are normalized. The live check changes the meaning of 'in line': Charter is now $131.52 (market value $18.6 billion, down about 67% from its 52-week high) and Cable One $36.44 (down about 80%) — the comp set has been repriced for structural decline since that note was written, so matching Charter's multiple is no longer a neutral statement, it is the market stamping a distressed-cable multiple on the entire Comcast conglomerate. That is precisely what the announced separation attacks: Disney ($95.87) and the bid-fought Warner Bros. Discovery ($26.61) show media, studio and parks assets commanding roughly twice the cable multiple when they trade on their own. Comcast at about 4.9 times consolidated enterprise value to operating cash earnings, with roughly 2.4 times net-debt leverage versus Charter's roughly 4 times, is the least-levered way to own the cable de-rate — and the only one with $12 billion of media and parks earnings inside the wrapper waiting to be re-labeled.
forcing_function: Three dated events force the re-rating. Largest: completion of the tax-free spin-off of NBCUniversal and Sky, announced June 29, 2026 with an expected completion around mid-2027 — the securities filings that precede a distribution (the Form 10 registration, debt allocation, dividend policies for each company, record date) are the hard markers through late 2026 and early 2027, and management has an on-schedule precedent in the Versant spin completed as promised at the end of 2025. Second: the second-quarter earnings call on July 23, 2026 — the first call since the separation announcement — which carries the initial separation detail, the first evidence on free-mobile-line cohorts converting to paid (management says early cohorts show 'a significant majority' rolling to paid), and Peacock's guided first-ever profitable quarter. Third: the second-half-2026 inflection management has staked itself to — free-line conversions lifting broadband revenue per customer and connectivity earnings improving off the investment trough — which, if delivered, converts the turnaround from promise to print before the spin even completes.
moderator_conclusion: This is a real sum-of-the-parts discount with a real, announced separation behind it, and the timing question is the only thing keeping it from an aggressive stance. Where we disagree with the market: at $23.63 the stock has fully round-tripped the June 29 separation pop, meaning the market is assigning roughly zero value to a board-committed, tax-free breakup with named chief executives and an on-schedule precedent — while pricing the parks, studios, Peacock and Sky at the same distressed-cable multiple as the broadband business. The street's consensus target of about $31 roughly matches our $30 base case, yet positioning is washed out (a smart-money score of 14 out of 100, analyst targets drifting down about 7% year over year, the stock 14% below its 200-day average and only about 7% off its 52-week low). The risky window over the next three to nine months is well defined: the July 23 print lands in the self-declared trough of the largest broadband investment year in the company's history with earnings per share expected down roughly 22%, the cable sector around it is still de-rating violently (Charter down about 67% from its high), and the separation's unanswered questions — debt split, dividend policy for two companies, index flowback when the media company is distributed — will all surface through the Form 10 process and could each produce a better entry. Mechanical-selling risk is real but bounded: the 5.6% yield attracts income holders who could exit if the successor payout policies disappoint, though the June washout already flushed much of the weak hand. The call: wait for the wash-out, one notch below an aggressive entry. The specific events to wait for — the July 23, 2026 second-quarter print (enter on any investment-phase flush toward the $22 June low), or the Form 10 filing that hardens the spin timeline, whichever comes first; either event with broadband trends intact converts this to an immediate entry. On management: a deep dive across five quarters of calls scores credibility 4 out of 5 — they pre-announced their own earnings decline, delivered the Versant spin on schedule, beat estimates every quarter, and were unusually candid about losing in the marketplace before fixing it — with the company's trajectory best described as turning: a deliberate self-breakup after two decades of conglomerate assembly. The value case stands on its own without the catalyst (a narrow but real scale moat in broadband, stable 71.7% gross margins, an 8-of-9 fundamental-health score, and free cash flow covering the dividend roughly four times), but the moat's edges are eroding under fiber and fixed-wireless attack and the media assets face a structural decline in linear television — which is exactly why the separation, not the operations, is what forces the value question to an answer.

skeptic_self.kill_fact: Four corrections were applied before scoring. (1) The screener's value anchors are inflated by one-time items: reported fiscal-2025 earnings of $5.39 per share (+30%) embed tax benefits and gains — the adjusted quarterly series (1.09/1.25/1.12/0.84) was flat year over year at about $4.30, and Q1 2026 adjusted earnings fell about 28% — so the scan's 127% margin of safety and $54 fair value were rejected in favor of a $30 sum-of-the-parts built on adjusted figures. (2) The scan's $100.96B net debt was replaced with the live-corrected $85.14B from the March 2026 balance sheet, and its grant-inflated insider signal was replaced with the real open-market record (zero buys, three sells). (3) Segment operating earnings in the sum-of-the-parts are estimates (the inputs supply only segment revenue), carrying roughly a ±15% band — hence a $28-33 working range rather than a point. (4) The separation is an announced intention, not a signed contract: no Form 10 is on file yet, and the roughly-one-year timeline rests on management's word — though the identical Versant playbook was announced in late 2024 and delivered on schedule, which is why the catalyst is graded as a firm, scheduled event rather than a soft one. A fifth check — whether the live collapse of Charter (down about 67%) and Cable One (down about 80%) reveals a terminal cable bear case rather than a de-rate — was weighed and partially absorbed: it lowered the broadband multiple to 5.25 times and set the bear case below the 52-week low, and it is the main reason conviction was tempered from 5 to 4 and the stance held at wait-for-the-washout rather than immediate entry. No prior-record block was present in the inputs, so no continuity adjustment was applied.
